It is not a mobility simulation: ASTERIA does not predict whether a rover can traverse a slope or surface.What VIPER is: NASA's Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover, built to map the location of water ice and other potential resources at the Moon's South Pole on a 100-day mission (NASA VIPER mission page).Published facts used here (NASA: VIPER rover and instruments): 2.5 m (8 ft) tall, 1.5 m (5 ft) long and wide; four wheel modules with active suspension and independent steering; headlights; a 1 m drill (TRIDENT); instruments NSS (neutron spectrometer), NIRVSS (near-infrared volatiles spectrometer) and MSolo (mass spectrometer). These follow the general appearance of NASA's published VIPER pictures, not measured drawings. No NASA images, textures or markings are used. VIPER's mass is not shown.Current status (NASA, 20 October 2026): VIPER "will embark on a mission to the lunar South Pole region in 2027"; it is "currently at NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston where it is fully built and undergoing final testing before traveling to NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida for launch to the Moon", to be delivered by a Blue Origin Blue Moon Mark 1 lander. Earlier: on 19 September 2025 NASA selected Blue Origin to deliver VIPER in late 2027 (NASA release; NASA's VIPER page names Mons Mouton as the destination); on 17 July 2024 NASA had announced its intent to discontinue VIPER, citing cost increases and launch delays (NASA release).In this view: each wheel rests on the LOLA surface under it and the body's pitch and roll follow from those four heights (Calculated from the DEM at its resolution - 20 m, or 5 m in the patch - so the tilt is the DEM's slope over about one cell; real ground under a rover is rougher). No traction, slip, power, wheel-soil or obstacle physics. The slope warning only compares the DEM slope with the limit you set.
